title: Fervor de Buenos Aires
significance: His self-published first poetry collection. Taking the back alleys of the outskirts and the city at evening as its material, it drew Buenos Aires — the stage for the rest of his life — as poetic terrain before anything else.

title: A Universal History of Infamy
significance: His first prose collection, rewriting the biographies of real swindlers and pirates as if they were encyclopedia entries. Borges's characteristic detour — summarizing and twisting other people's stories to make his own narrative — begins here.

title: Ficciones
significance: His major story collection, bringing together "The Library of Babel" and "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote." Through the form of a review of a book that does not exist, it changed the very idea of what length fiction needs.

title: The Aleph
significance: The title story, in which the narrator witnesses in a basement a sphere where every point in the universe appears superimposed in one place, anchors a gathering of stories on infinity, memory, and betrayal. It is the densest single collection of Borges's metaphysical fiction.

title: Other Inquisitions
significance: A prose collection gathering short essays such as "Kafka and His Precursors" and "John Wilkins' Analytical Language." It best shows why the distinction between fiction and essay becomes meaningless in his writing.

title: The Book of Sand
significance: A late-life story collection containing the title story, about a book whose pages multiply infinitely so that it has neither a findable beginning nor end. It is the result of retesting his early devices in a drier prose.

title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
significance: His second poetry collection, published around age twenty. By overlaying the feelings of love onto the terrain of the sea, the forest, and the night, it became the most widely read poetry collection in the Spanish-speaking world.

title: Residence on Earth
significance: A turning point at which he abandoned his early lyricism for difficult images cataloguing the decay of matter and the wear of time. It reappeared in an expanded edition in Madrid in 1935, shocking the Spanish poetry world of the day.

title: Spain in Our Hearts
significance: A poetry collection written after he witnessed the massacres of the Spanish Civil War. It marks the point where he moved from private lyricism to public testimony, and all of Neruda's later political poetry branches out from here.

title: Canto General
significance: A fifteen-part long epic poem that starts from the geology and plant life of the American continent and sweeps through conquest, dictatorship, and mine labor. It was completed while he was a political fugitive and appeared in Mexico and Chile the same year.

title: Elemental Odes
significance: A series applying the classical ode form to everyday objects like onions, tomatoes, and socks. With short lines and plain vocabulary, it widened the list of things poetry could take as its subject.

title: Isla Negra: A Notebook
significance: A five-volume autobiographical poetry collection published at age sixty. Retracing everything from his childhood in the southern forests to his political career in chronological order, it is his own accounting of the changes in his style.

title: The Burning Plain
significance: A story collection set in the rural Jalisco of the post-revolutionary years. In a spoken idiom where the narrator never explains his own situation, it established a way of writing that recorded violence and poverty without emotional intrusion.

title: Pedro Páramo
significance: A short novel in which a son arrives in Comala looking for his dead father and realizes he has entered a town of the already-dead. By crossing speakers and timelines with no markers, it places the voices of the living and the dead on the same level.

title: The Golden Cockerel
significance: A novella written in the 1950s as a text for film and published as a standalone book some twenty years later. Following the rise and fall of a cockfighting gambler, it shows how Rulfo's spoken idiom operates within popular narrative.

title: Bestiario
significance: His first story collection. Something unidentified taking over a house, or a character vomiting up rabbits, is narrated with no explanation at all, and his basic template for handling the moment when the surface of daily life cracks open is completed here.

title: Final del juego
significance: His second story collection, gathering stories in which games and their rules encroach on reality. It was expanded after its first edition, and many of Cortázar's best-known stories ended up gathered in this book.

title: Las armas secretas
significance: A story collection containing "The Pursuer," about the final period of a jazz saxophonist's life. "The Devil's Drool," in which the interpretation of a single photograph keeps sliding, became the source for Antonioni's film Blow-Up.

title: Cronopios and Famas
significance: A collection of short prose mixing the invented species of cronopios and famas with instruction-manual pieces like "Instructions for Climbing a Staircase." In a form that is neither fiction nor essay, it is the book where his humor shows most directly.

title: Hopscotch
significance: A novel that sets aside a separate group of "expendable chapters" after the main text and offers two reading orders. By inserting theoretical fragments into a story that moves between Paris and Buenos Aires, it made the novel comment on itself.

title: Music in Cuba
significance: A study tracing the formation of Cuban music from the colonial period to the twentieth century as a crossing of African and European elements. The rhythm and contrapuntal construction of his later novels grew out of this musicological training.

title: The Kingdom of This World
significance: A short novel following the Haitian Revolution through the eyes of the enslaved Ti Noël. It comes with a prologue arguing that in the Americas the marvelous already exists as fact, so that a manifesto and a novel form a single book.

title: The Lost Steps
significance: A journey in which a city musicologist searches for primitive instruments and travels upriver into the jungle, moving backward through time itself. It drives forward as a first-person account of reaching the origin and then losing the way back.

title: Explosion in a Cathedral
significance: A novel depicting the arrival of the French Revolution's ideas and its guillotine together in the Caribbean, seen through young people in Havana and the historical figure Victor Hugues. It makes what the revolution turns into within a colony the axis of its narrative.

title: Baroque Concerto
significance: A short novel in which a wealthy Mexican and his servant arrive in Venice and are drawn into an improvised performance among composers of the day. By deliberately placing anachronisms, it overturns the rules of the historical novel.

title: Sagarana
significance: A collection of nine novellas and stories set in the sertão of Minas Gerais. It brings dialect and the rhythms of oral storytelling into its sentences while still keeping to standard syntax, showing the point where Rosa's linguistic experimentation begins.

title: The Devil to Pay in the Backlands
significance: A novel that runs entirely as a single spoken account, without chapter breaks, that the old gunman Riobaldo pours out to an unnamed visitor. Sentences built up out of dialect and neologism, together with a structure that never settles whether his pact with the devil was real, reset the standard for Brazilian fiction.

title: The Third Bank of the River and Other Stories
significance: A collection of short pieces repeatedly experimenting with ways of seeing the world made strange, borrowing the viewpoints of children and the insane. "The Third Bank of the River," about a father who takes to the middle of a river and never returns, is included in this book.

title: Tutaméia: Terceiras estórias
significance: His last book, arranging short stories together with several prefaces in alphabetical order. Compression and omission are pushed to an extreme, so that each piece comes close to being a riddle.

title: Near to the Wild Heart
significance: Her first novel, published at age twenty-three. It follows Joana's childhood and marriage with no chronological order, tracking only the movement of consciousness, breaking from the convention of the Brazilian fiction of the time, which portrayed place and society.

title: Family Ties
significance: A story collection repeatedly built around the moment when a character, in one everyday scene, suddenly grasps the structure of her own life. Short stories such as "Love" and "The Hen" later became the standard by which Lispector is read.

title: The Passion According to G.H.
significance: A novel that stretches a few minutes of encountering a cockroach in a maid's room into a book-length first-person meditation. Its structure, in which each chapter opens with the last sentence of the one before, turns the chaining of thought into form.

title: Água Viva
significance: Prose with no plot and no characters, chasing only the sensation of the moment of writing. In a form that gives up the distinctions between novel, poem, and diary, it shows the point her late-period sentences arrived at.

title: The Hour of the Star
significance: Her last novel, written in a structure where a male narrator, who is writing her, keeps interrupting the story of Macabéa, a typist who came up to Rio from the northeast. It brings the very difficulty of representing poverty inside the novel itself.
